newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Consumers seen as key to Australia telecoms opening.
newsitem.headline: Consumers seen as key to Australia telecoms opening.

text.p: The Australian government will use consumer benefit to measure the success of opening the country's telecommunications industry to full competition, Communications Minister Richard Alston said on Friday.
Alston predicted that one or two larger telecoms companies would dominate the market once deregulation took place on July 1, but said this was not a concern as long as consumers were seen to benefit.
"I think the real measure is whether you're getting significant price reductions and a better quality of service," Alston told reporters.
"I think we will have a few larger players dominating the market ... but that doesn't mean you can't have ferocious competition at the margins, particularly in regional areas.
"I think the measure is not market share as much as consumer benefit."

Australia took the first step towards telecoms deregulation in the early 1990s when it allowed a single competitor, Optus Communications Pty Ltd, to set up against government-owned monopoly Telstra Corp Ltd.
The former Labor government then allowed Vodaphone to set up a third mobile telephone network and targeted July 1, 1997, as the beginning of completely open competition within the industry.

Alston's Liberal-National administration last year set out the regulatory system for the new competitive regime, under which there would be no limit on the number of carrier licences issued and no restrictions on the services they could provide.
Alston said the government had not provided for a review of the deregulated market at any specific time, but rather would continuously monitor the market and deal with problems as they arose.
"If there's a problem you've got to fix it," he said.
"If a problem shows up in 12 months there's no point in saying we've got to wait another 12 months for our review."
Alston said the government expected telecoms carriers initially to cut telephone call charges a little, but the reductions would increase over time.
Telstra and Optus plan separate public listings in the first year of deregulation. The government is selling one third of Telstra, to raise an estimated A$8 billion (US$6 billion).
